campaign.lore/Places/Heron Warehouse (truth).md:
---
summary: "GM only: the truth about the Heron warehouse: the King's 'lost' grain re-sacked under the heron and barged downriver; why the true book exists (no honour among thieves, only bookkeeping) and what's in it, down to the goblins' pay; the night's routine (the land door for the Master at the midnight bell, the river door and Hobb's token, the count, the ebb); who pays for it and what each of the night staff stands to lose (Hep Grist's gang, Saul Tench, Mister Scrope); what would prove it; and the dangers (the river, the hoists, the grain dust, the Crakes)."
type: "place"
visibility: "gm"
---
# The Heron warehouse: the truth

This is where the King's grain goes. Wagons the Granary Roll calls "lost to goblins" come down the Wharf Road by night, still in the palace's wheat-ear sacks. The grain is re-sacked under the heron and sold downriver as Saltmere grain. The Heron's day book, which anyone may see, calls it condemned stock lawfully sold by the Royal Purveyor's office. Everyone who works here knows whose grain it is, and nobody says.

**Why the book exists**: Sallow doesn't trust the Saltmere factor, and the factor doesn't trust Sallow, so both insisted on a true book kept by a clerk they both pay, Mister Lemuel Scrope. There is no honour among thieves; there is bookkeeping. Every page records the "lost" wagons by their Granary Roll number and date, the sacks received in wheat-ear sacking, re-sacked and sold by the barge-load, the price and the Master's share, initialled "J.S." in the Master's hand. It balances, so it records what goes out of the factor's cashbox too: on the last page of each month, "Hedge-folk, the usual: forty heron pennies."

**The night's routine**
- On loading nights nobody comes in at the land door but the Master, at the midnight bell, with his lantern-boy and the Crake brothers. Saul holds the wicket for him and keeps Duchess off his ankles.
- The gang come and go by the river door, showing a brass heron token at its grille for whoever is nearest to draw the bolt. Hobb's token is on the string round his neck. A token is all it takes: whoever shows one is let in and handed a sack, since Hep is always short of hands.
- The hoist is worked from the floor, on a winch just inside the river door, its beam out over the barge: Hobb, on the hoist, is in among the gang, in view of the counting-box.
- Hep Grist shouts the count, Scrope enters every sack, and the Master checks it, initials the night's page and takes his share in heron pennies.
- The barge sails on the ebb, and at the end of the night the empty wheat-ear sacks go into the river, weighted with stones.

**Who pays for it**
- **Hep Grist's re-sacking gang** are on double pay and frightened of the gallows, because receiving the King's grain is a hanging matter. Hep skims a sack a night for the gang's families, and her son Kit is in the gang.
- **Saul Tench** is paid three times what the river watch paid him. He knows whose grain it is and minds his own business, and he'd sooner be on a sergeant's side than in front of a judge.
- **Mister Scrope** was Wendell Prout's oldest friend, and doesn't believe he hanged himself. A clerk who keeps an honest book for the Master might be next.
- **Hobb**, the Master's man on the hoist, stands to hang for the clerk as well as the grain.

Each of them, and what would turn them, is in their own GM notes in the cast.

**What would prove it**: the gang slitting wheat-ear sacks beside a stack of heron sacks; the heap of empties waiting for the river; the true book; the night staff, if they'll swear for the Crown; and the Master caught at the loading, which a sergeant may arrest him for on her own authority.

**Dangers**: the river in spate under the floor; the hoists; the grain dust hanging in the lantern light (NO NAKED LIGHTS, says the sign everyone ignores, and a flame in that dust goes up like gunpowder); and the Crakes, who'll put a man in the river for half a crown.

**In motion**: how the Master comes tonight (on time, wary or warned), and the Patience sailing at the second bell, are in [What's in motion](../World/Fronts.md).

campaign.lore/Places/Heron Warehouse.md:
---
summary: "The Heron warehouse, the last warehouse at the downriver end of Caerwyn's wharves: a tall tarred store half on piles over the river under a painted heron sign, the house mark of a Saltmere grain factor new to Caerwyn; why its sacks and its new silver heron pennies carry the heron (and why the pennies spend downriver but not in town); the land door with the old watchman, his brazier and his mastiff, the river door and its grille along the plank walk, the hoists and the barges, double pay for night loading, and the dock talk about its busy nights."
type: "place"
visibility: "public"
---
# The Heron warehouse

The last warehouse at the downriver end of the wharves, where the lamps give out. You notice a tall, tarred timber store standing half on the wharf and half on piles over the river; a painted heron on its signboard; and a brazier at its land door, with an old watchman beside it and a vast dog asleep across the threshold.

**Why the heron**: Saltmere lets its great merchant houses strike their own silver, each with its house mark, and a house's mark downriver is as good as its name. The heron is the mark of one Saltmere grain factor, new to Caerwyn this season, who took the last warehouse on the wharf and hung out his sign. Sacks go out of it stamped with the heron, and his people are paid in new silver pennies with a heron where the King's face should be. Nobody on the river had seen one before this month. A heron penny spends without a blink in Saltmere; in Caerwyn the chandlers want the King's face. Saltmere's own banner is the salt-gull, not the heron.

**What's here**
- **The land door**: big double doors with a wicket in one leaf, facing the wharf and the foot of the Wharf Road, with the watchman's sentry box and brazier beside it.
- **The river door**: a low loading door at water level with a grille in it, reached along a slippery plank walk on the piles.
- **Hoists** jutting out over the water, and barges moored alongside to load straight from the store.
- After dark, lantern light shows through the cracks in the boards, and a lamp burns in a high window.

**Who's about, and why**
- **Old Saul**, the night watchman, with a lantern, a rattle and opinions about loiterers. He used to walk the river for the river watch. His mastiff, Duchess, knows everyone who works there by smell.
- **Porters in grain-white** on loading nights, at double pay.
- **Saltmere bargees**, who care about the tide and nothing else. The factor himself never comes to Caerwyn.

**What it needs, trades and resents**: it needs strong hands on loading nights, and pays double for them in heron silver. It trades grain downriver to Saltmere. The wharf resents its barges going down full while Caerwyn goes short, and takes its pay all the same. It doesn't care for questions.

**The rules of the place, and who keeps them**: the watchman keeps the land door, and on a loading night his orders are to let nobody in by it. The night gang come and go by the river door. One lantern hangs at the land door on an ordinary night; when the Heron is expecting trouble there are two, and men walk the wharf with a third.

**How the town's troubles show here**: barges going downriver low in the water while bread is dear, and porters on double pay who still can't afford a loaf.

**What's happening now**: dock talk says the Heron has been busy at night all this past month. A broad Saltmere barge, the Patience, lies alongside, and the ebb runs at the second bell after midnight.

campaign.lore/Places/Market Square.md:
---
summary: "Caerwyn's market square and the Corn Exchange: the procession route hung with bunting and the delegations' banners, stalls, bakers and bread queues, the market cross and its preacher, the Corn Exchange's price board chalked at the noon and evening bells, the grain factors and Saltmere buyers, Abel Fennick the Exchange's clerk and the wagon lists he keeps in the back rooms, sweepers and watchmen, and how the square changes from the eve of the Assembly to procession morning."
type: "place"
visibility: "public"
---
# The market square and the Corn Exchange

The middle of Caerwyn, between the palace on the rise, the granary quarter and the top of the river stairs. You notice the square half hung with bunting and half scaffolded for tomorrow's procession; the Corn Exchange's price board, with people stopped in front of it; and the bread queue.

**What's here**
- **The procession route**, across the square from the palace road to the far side, lined with bunting and the delegations' banners, with sweepers on it.
- **Stalls**: bakers, a pieman, chandlers, and anyone else with something to sell before the square shuts for the procession.
- **The market cross**: stone steps where criers cry and preachers preach.
- **The Corn Exchange**, a columned hall on one side of the square. Its price board hangs outside. In the front hall the factors trade grain by the sample, and the back rooms are where the Exchange keeps its wagon lists: every load of grain sold in the city, weighed and entered, by the cart and by the sack.
- **Streets off it**: up the rise to the palace gate, along to the granary quarter, and down to the top of the river stairs.

**Who's about, and why**
- **Market folk and stallholders**, who want to sell up before the procession shuts the square.
- **Bakers and their queues.** The bakers want flour they can afford; the queues want bread they can afford.
- **Grain factors**, Saltmere buyers among them, who want their price.
- **Abel Fennick**, the Exchange's clerk, who chalks up the board and keeps the wagon lists. He wants the lists straight and the factors happy.
- **Sweepers, and watchmen lining the route**, moving carts and chasing pigs.
- **Delegations' servants**, buying for their masters.

**What it needs, trades and resents**: it needs the square clear for the procession by morning. It trades in everything, and in grain by the sample. It resents the price board, and the procession that will shut the market tomorrow.

**The rules of the place, and who keeps them**
- **The price board** is chalked at the noon bell and again at the evening bell. The factors set the prices, and Fennick chalks them up.
- **The wagon lists** are for the factors and the palace's own clerks. Fennick shows them to nobody else without a factor's word or the Purveyor's seal, and this week every other answer is "After the Assembly".
- **Short weight** is the market warden's to fine, and the market warden is at the palace this week.
- **The route** is the watch's: carts off it, pigs off it, and nothing left on it overnight.

**How the town's troubles show here**: the board, the queues and the smaller loaves; the bunting and the banners going up over people who can't afford bread; "lost to goblins" said at every stall about anything missing. And a preacher at the market cross calls dear bread a judgement on the bunting.

**What's happening now**: the eve of the Assembly. The banners go up, the noon price is chalked up, and by evening it's up again with something rude written beside it. At night the square is empty but for the sweepers and a watchman asleep upright against a lamppost. On procession morning the crowd lines the route from first light.

**Room to improvise**: stallholders, the pieman, the criers, the preacher's text. Tie each to the bread, the Assembly or the goblins.

campaign.lore/Places/Palace Kitchens.md:
---
summary: "The palace kitchens in the back courts: Mistress Pruett the cook, the Assembly feast in the making for four delegations, flour short since the palace's own wagons went 'lost to goblins', deliveries from the Royal Purveyor's office through the service entrance and what the kitchens think of them and their wheat-ear silver, gossip up from the river with the eels, extra hands fed for scrubbing, and a place where a child carrying a bucket goes unquestioned."
type: "place"
visibility: "public"
---
# The palace kitchens

Vaulted kitchens off the kitchen yard in the palace's back courts: spits, bread ovens, a pastry room, cold larders and a scullery. You notice more heat, steam and shouting than anywhere else in Caerwyn, a feast for four delegations in the making, and the cook in the middle of it.

**What's here**: the spits and bread ovens; the pastry room; the cold larders; the scullery; and the kitchen yard, where deliveries come in from the service entrance.

**Who's about, and why**
- **Mistress Pruett**, the palace cook, who runs the kitchens like a warship and hears everything. She wants the feast on the table at the hour the Marshal has written down, and every dish fit to set before four delegations.
- **Cooks, scullions and kitchen boys**, and on a feast day **extra hands**: the kitchens take anyone who'll scrub, turn a spit or carry a bucket, and feed them. Nobody asks a child with a bucket who they are.
- **The Purveyor's carters**, in and out of the kitchen yard with deliveries.

**What it needs, trades and resents**: it needs flour, and the office's wagons keep coming short. It trades scraps, and gossip, which comes up from the river with the eels and the fish and goes out again with the scraps. It resents the Royal Purveyor's office: its deliveries, its under-purveyors, and its purse silver, stamped with a wheat-ear so that the kitchens can't pinch it.

**The rules of the place, and who keeps them**: Mistress Pruett's word is law below stairs. Deliveries come in by the service entrance and are counted in the kitchen yard. Office silver is the office's, and a kitchen hand caught with a wheat-ear coin has some explaining to do.

**How the town's troubles show here**: the palace's own grain has been "lost to goblins", so the feast's bread is being baked from what the office could find, and the office has promised the rest by morning. The cushions haven't arrived either, and the under-purveyor for linen has been seen in the kitchen yard asking after them.

**What's happening now**: the eve of the Assembly. The feast is being cooked through the night for tomorrow, after the Assembly sits.

campaign.lore/Places/River Stairs.md:
---
summary: "The river stairs and the docks of Caerwyn: the long wet steps down from the quay to the wharves, the landings and the pump, the Drowned Rat halfway down, the Wharf Road for wagons, warehouses with hoists and river doors (the Heron the last of them), dock-porters, lightermen, bargees, eel-sellers and mudlarks, Saltmere barges and their factors' pay, the river watch who walk the stairs in fours, the river in winter spate, the docks after dark, and the river paid off early because the docks shut for the procession."
type: "place"
visibility: "public"
---
# The river stairs and the docks

The river stairs run from the quay at the bottom of the town down the steep bank to the wharves. You notice the worn stone steps, wet and green all winter; the porters waiting on the landings with their hooks and coils of rope; and the river at the bottom, brown and fast by day and black by night. Nobody has ever counted the same number of steps twice.

**What's here**
- **The landings**, where porters wait for work, and a **pump** on one of them, where they wash.
- **The Drowned Rat**, dug into the bank on a landing halfway down.
- **The wharves** along the river at the foot of the stairs. The warehouses have hoists jutting out over the water and river doors at water level, so barges can load straight from the store. The grain warehouses are at the downriver end, where the lamps give out, and the Heron is the last of them.
- **The Wharf Road**, which winds down the bank behind the warehouses at the downriver end: the way wagons get to the wharves, since nothing on wheels can take the stairs.
- **The river**, in winter spate: high, fast and freezing. What goes in at the wharves comes out at the sea, or doesn't.

**Who's about, and why**
- **Dock-porters**: big men, paid by the load, who drink it by the night.
- **Lightermen and bargees**, working the barges in the stream and moored at the foot of the stairs.
- **Eel-sellers**, and **mudlarks** picking the mud at low water for anything worth a penny.
- **Saltmere factors' clerks**, who pay best and ask least.

**What it needs, trades and resents**: the docks live on loads, and the Saltmere factors pay best: the Heron pays double for night loading and doesn't care for questions. Porters grumble about Saltmere barges going downriver full while Caerwyn goes short, and take Saltmere's money anyway.

**The rules, and who keeps them**: the stairs are the river watch's patch. The river watch walks them in fours after dark, or not at all. What a man does on the stairs is the river's business.

**How the town's troubles show here**: bread is dear, so the stew on the stairs is thin and the night work is welcome. Saltmere barges go downriver low in the water. And the docks shut for the procession tomorrow, so the river loses a day's pay.

**After dark** the wharves are black and quiet but for the odd barge loading by lantern. The watch comes down only when it must.

**What's happening now**: the eve of the Assembly. The docks shut tomorrow for the procession, so the river pays off early this evening and the Rat is full by dusk. The river watch is up on the Assembly route with the rest of the watch. At the downriver end a broad Saltmere barge lies alongside the Heron, and the ebb runs at the second bell after midnight, as every bargee knows.

**Room to improvise**: porters and their nicknames, what the mudlarks find, a lighterman's grudge about mooring fines. Tie each to dear bread, Saltmere money or the procession.

campaign.lore/Places/The Drowned Rat (truth).md:
---
summary: "GM only: the truth in the Drowned Rat on the eve of the Assembly: Big Hobb, Sallow's frightened muscle and the big man with the bandaged hand (the rope burn, the token, the heron pennies he's losing at cards); who in the room knows or has guessed what (Nan Quill, Dilly Sparrow and her brandy, Arlo at the pump, Cob in the scullery); the Crake brothers, barred from the Rat; what would prove it; and what may come down the stairs tonight."
type: "place"
visibility: "gm"
---
# The Drowned Rat: the truth

**Big Hobb Mallory** is Sallow's muscle and the big man with the bandaged hand. The tarry rag on his right hand covers a rope burn from hauling Prout up on the sack hoist. He drinks here every night, and harder since. He isn't a killer by nature. He's frightened of the Master, of what he did, and of the hand being seen, so he keeps it under the table. He knows the loft, the Master's name, and the Heron's night routine, and the brass token for its river door hangs on the greasy string round his neck. His own truth, and what would open him, is in [his GM notes](../Cast/Big%20Hobb%20Mallory/gm.md).

**Who in the room knows what**
- **Nan Quill** knows the gentleman Hobb works for is Master Sallow, and won't sell it at any price. She has put this morning's hanged clerk together with Hobb's hand and the night he went out before the midnight bells, and she wants none of it in her house.
- **Dilly Sparrow** has won the best part of three shillings in heron pennies off Hobb, who has been playing to lose since last night. He told her he's due at the Heron at the eleventh bell and would sooner be dead. She thinks he's mixed up in smuggling. She has six casks of Saltmere brandy under the onions on the Dabchick, run past the King's tide-waiters, and is certain any sergeant in the Rat has come for them.
- **Arlo Quarry** saw Hobb unwrap the hand at the pump on the stairs this evening: the palm is skinned raw in a stripe straight across. He's saving it to shame Hobb with if Hobb refuses him the third time.
- **Cob** knows the big cove from the loft by his size and his "Yes, Master". He's been hiding in the scullery since Hobb came in.
- **The Crake brothers**, two river-bruisers alike as two bollards (only one of them talks), are barred from the Rat: rule three, once each. Somebody hires them for the Heron's wharf on loading nights.

**What would prove it here**: Hobb's palm; the token on his string; the heron pennies in Nan's jar, on Dilly's table and in Cob's pocket; Hobb's own words; Arlo's account of the pump; and Cob, who would point him out from behind something.

**In motion**: whether anyone comes asking down the stairs tonight, and what Hobb's master does if Hobb runs to him, is in [What's in motion](../World/Fronts.md) under "The Purveyor's man".

---
summary: "The Drowned Rat, a dockside dive halfway down the river stairs: Nan Quill the landlady and her blackthorn cudgel Manners, the rules board by the door (no credit, no blades out, no fighting indoors, no watch on duty, no singing before the ninth bell, what's said in the Rat stays in the Rat, gossip sold by the measure) and what breaking a rule costs, gossip at a gill, a half or a pint (never a quart), ale, gin and eel stew, Tuppenny Bargee at Dilly Sparrow's table, arm-wrestling for the champion's chair, the regulars (Big Hobb, Arlo Quarry, dock-porters and bargees), Cob the pot-boy, and a full house on the eve of the Assembly."
type: "place"
visibility: "public"
---
# The Drowned Rat

A dockside dive dug into the bank on a landing halfway down the river stairs, three steps down from the landing to its one door. Inside it's one long, low, smoky room under a ceiling hung with eel traps and old oars, with a scullery at the back. You notice the rules board just inside the door; the driftwood fire burning blue with salt in the corner; and, behind a bar made from the upturned hull of a skiff, the original drowned rat floating in a great jar of gin. It has been there longer than Nan.

**What's here**
- **The door**: the only way in or out, onto the stairs. It was rehung twenty years ago, after Nan put a constable of the watch out through it: through it, not the doorway.
- **The bar**, with Manners on two nails behind it and a row of pewter measures on hooks, from a gill to a quart, used for beer and gossip alike. Under it is a jar marked FOREIGN, where Nan keeps money she can't spend in town.
- **The champion's chair** by the fire, the Rat's only armchair. It's kept for whoever is arm-wrestling champion of the river stairs, and nobody else sits in it, not even Nan.
- **Dilly Sparrow's card table** by the fire, a long table and benches on the floor, and a corner table with its back to the wall.
- **The scullery**: pots, steam and eel stew, and a slop hatch over the river, just big enough for a boy. The river under it is fast and cold.

**The rules of the house**, painted by the door in Nan's own capitals so that nobody can say they didn't see it:

> THE DROWNED RAT. RULES OF THE HOUSE. 1. No credit. 2. No blades out. 3. No fighting indoors. 4. No watch on duty. 5. No singing before the ninth bell. 6. What's said in the Rat stays in the Rat. 7. Gossip sold by the measure. By order, N. Quill. Enforced by Manners.

Nan enforces them to the letter, with Manners. There's one warning for small things (a raised voice, a threat, a song before the ninth bell) and none for a fist or a blade. After the warning comes Manners and the door, and you're barred until Nan says otherwise. Nobody is stopped at her door: outside it is the river's business. Nan sees no contradiction between rules six and seven, since the gossip is sold in the Rat. A watchman off duty may drink like anyone, if he pays.

**Gossip by the measure**: money on the bar first, then Nan takes the measure off its hook and talks until it's full. A gill (a penny) buys what everyone on the stairs knows; a half (tuppence), what most don't; a pint (fourpence), what only Nan knows. She doesn't sell quarts: a quart'll get you drowned. Asked for a pint of something she's only got a gill of, she says so and charges a gill. She sells what she knows, never what she's guessed.

**The house custom**: elbows on the table, right hands, Nan referees, and wagers are paid at the bar. Anyone may challenge the champion. A champion who refuses three challenges in one night gives up the chair, and it goes to the challenger.

**Who's about, and why**
- **Nan Quill**, the landlady: a small, square woman of sixty who calls everyone "my duck". She wants a full, paying, peaceful house and her rules kept.
- **The regulars**: dock-porters, lightermen, bargees and carters, here to drink their pay. A great many of them are big men, and a good few are bandaged somewhere: it's the docks.
- **Big Hobb Mallory**, champion of the Rat at the arm-wrestling these eleven years, in the fireside corner every night.
- **Dilly Sparrow**, an ancient bargewoman, dealing Tuppenny Bargee by the fire for tuppence a hand. Her barge, the Dabchick, is tied up at the foot of the stairs.
- **Arlo Quarry**, a young lighterman by the door, who'll arm-wrestle anyone for anything and wants the champion's chair.
- **Cob**, a granary boy, who does Nan's pots on busy nights for a penny and a bowl of eel stew. Nan barred his da years ago for hitting him.

**What it needs, trades and resents**: it needs a full house and no blood on the floor, because the river watch could shut the Rat over blood. It trades in ale, gin, eel stew, cards and gossip. It resents the watch on duty, and the four shillings and sixpence the watch still owes for the door.

**How the town's troubles show here**: dear bread means thinner eel stew, and Nan charges the same. New silver from the night work at the Heron crosses the bar and goes in the jar. And with the docks shut tomorrow for the procession, the whole river is here tonight.

**What's happening now**: the eve of the Assembly. By dusk the Rat is packed with porters, lightermen and bargees, paid off early because the docks shut tomorrow.

**Room to improvise**: regulars and their grudges, the songs that start at the ninth bell, the history of the rat in the jar. Tie each to the river, dear bread or the house rules.

summary: "The watch house at the edge of the granary quarter: the lamp over the door, the front counter and its bell, the notice board with the Assembly notices and the Purveyor's office's delivery notices, Sergeant Kell's desk, the two cells, the cold room in the cellar where the murdered dead wait for the surgeon, the dead-cart in the back yard, who's about in Assembly week (mostly nobody), and who might be in the cells or under a sheet tonight."
type: "place"

# The watch house

A narrow brick watch house at the edge of the granary quarter. You notice the lamp over the door, which burns all night; the bell on the front counter, to ring when nobody's behind it (this week, always); and the quiet.

**What's here**
- **The front room**: the counter and its bell, benches, and a board of notices. Alongside the usual thieves and lost dogs, this week the board carries the order of procession, the Marshal's arms order, and the Purveyor's office's Assembly delivery notices, signed "J. Sallow, for the Royal Purveyor".
- **The sergeants' room** behind it, where Sergeant Kell's desk is the tidiest thing in the building.
- **Two cells**, usually with a drunk in one.
- **The cold room** in the cellar, once an ice house, where the murdered dead wait for the watch surgeon. A body comes in only when a sergeant signs for it.
- **The back yard**, where the dead-cart and its long ladder are kept.

**Who's about, and why**: Sergeant Agnes Kell, when she isn't out; Corporal Abner Tull and his two constables, when they aren't on the route; in Assembly week, mostly nobody. The Captain works from the palace this week.

**What it needs, trades and resents**: it needs men, and the surgeon back from the palace. It trades in reports, which the Captain likes short. It resents the Assembly route, and the river stairs, which it leaves to the river watch.

**The rules of the place, and who keeps them**: the Captain's book says how each death is filed. A sergeant signs a body into the cold room, and answers for it. Whoever brings a prisoner in locks him up and keeps the key, because this week there's nobody to leave it with.

**How the town's troubles show here**: the Assembly has emptied it; the procession notices cover the board; and the dead-cart goes out to the north gate on the Captain's say-so.

**What's happening now**: the eve of the Assembly, and the whole watch is on the route through the night. Who is in the cold room or the cells depends on how the day has gone: the clerk from the granary, if a sergeant signed him in as a murder; anyone taken in since.

---
summary: "How Caerwyn stands right now, hour by hour, from the morning a clerk was found hanged behind the King's Granary to the morning of the Assembly procession: the bells, the price of bread, the Corn Exchange board, the Assembly preparations, the palace gate, the river and the watch, the talk around town and who's saying it (porters, carters, market folk, the palace kitchens, the stairs), and what the town says about the King's investigator. Kept up to date as the story goes on."
type: "world"
visibility: "public"
---
# Caerwyn now

What anyone in town could see or hear, hour by hour, on the eve of the Centennial Assembly and the morning after. Go by the scene's time and by what has actually happened: an "If" line holds only if it did. Talk belongs to the people named, and is said once, by someone it matters to.

## Morning, the eve
- **The town**: bunting going up on every rope that will hold it, and the whole watch out lining the procession route. Every official is at the palace, and the answer to every request is "After the Assembly."
- **Bread**: tuppence a loaf, a penny dearer than at harvest, with queues at the bakers since first light. The Corn Exchange chalks up the day's prices at the noon bell.
- **The talk**:
  - Granary porters: a palace clerk hanged himself off the sack hoist behind the King's Granary. The Captain says so, and the dead-cart comes at noon.
  - Carters: nobody takes the King's Road after dark, with the patrols all called in to line the route.
  - Dock-porters: the docks shut tomorrow for the procession, so the river pays off early tonight.
  - The palace kitchens: the under-purveyor for linen is having a very bad week about the King's cushions.

## Afternoon, the eve
- **The town**: the route swept, the delegations' banners up round the market square, rehearsals at the palace. The palace gate takes written messages for the Marshal, who reads them by evening.
- **Bread**: the noon price on the Corn Exchange board is up again, and people stop to read it and grumble. A preacher at the market cross is calling dear bread a judgement on the bunting.
- **The clerk**:
  - If he went out on the dead-cart as a suicide: its bell goes through the market towards the north gate, and nobody looks up. He's in the pit by sundown.
  - If a sergeant signed him in as a murder: he went to the watch house under a sheet, not out of the north gate, and the granary porters tell anyone that a sergeant signed him in over the Captain's word.
  - If a granary child was taken in for it: the market says a granary brat did for the clerk and the watch has the child. The granary rats say otherwise, loudly.
- **The talk**: travellers at the gates grumbling about the Treasury's shilling a head; palace porters saying the King's cushions are still stuck in the wagon queue at the service entrance.

## Evening, the eve
- **The town**: lamps lit along the procession route. The palace is shut to everyone but the delegations' dinner and the procession rehearsal, and the King sees no one before morning.
- **Bread**: the evening chalking is up again since noon, and someone has written something rude beside it. The same tuppence buys a smaller loaf, and stew on the river stairs is thinner.
- **The river**: paid off early, so the Drowned Rat and every dive on the stairs is full by dusk. The river watch is up on the route with everyone else.
- **The talk**: on the stairs, Saltmere barges have been loading at the Heron by night all month and going downriver low in the water, while bread goes up.

## Night, the eve
- **The town**: the watch lines the route through the night. The market square is empty but for sweepers and a watchman asleep upright against a lamppost.
- **The river**: high and black, with fog coming off it after the eleventh bell, when the night porters go down to the shifts. At the downriver end the Heron's hoist is working over the Saltmere barge Patience, which sails on the ebb at the second bell after midnight.
- **The talk**: the Heron's gang grumble that they're on double pay and still can't buy bread.

## Procession morning
- **The town**: bells, a band tuning up, bunting everywhere, and the delegations forming up under their banners in the palace courtyard. At the ninth bell the procession leaves the palace gate for the market square, the Purveyor's party walking fourth with a grain cart in garlands, "for the people's confidence". The docks are shut.
- **Bread**: threepence, at the bakers who open.
- **The talk**:
  - Along the route: people who've come to shout "lost to goblins!" at the Purveyor's grain cart.
  - If the Heron burned or its barge sank in the night: the whole waterfront saw it, and "lost to goblins" has become "lost to fire".
  - If an under-purveyor was taken up at the wharves in the night: the palace porters have it by breakfast, and the Captain says he suspected the man all along.
  - If the barge sailed: the Heron's doors are shut, its floor is swept, and nobody on the wharves saw anything.

## The King's investigator
What Caerwyn says about them, a line for each public deed as it gets about, with who's saying it. To begin with nobody knows them, though the palace gate has been told the King will see them in the morning.

campaign.lore/World/Caerwyn.md:
---
summary: "The city of Caerwyn and King Aldren's court: why the city lives on the King's Road and the river, its quarters (the palace on the rise, the market square and Corn Exchange, the granary quarter, the river stairs and docks, the Shambles, the north gate with the Mending House and the suicides' pit), bells, money and wages, magic, the law and who keeps it, who does well and who goes short, what people say, and the city on the eve of the Centennial Assembly."
type: "world"
visibility: "public"
---
# Caerwyn

The King's city, where the King's Road meets the river: grain comes in by road and goes out by barge, and the palace on the rise lives off both. This winter it's host to the Centennial Assembly, and everything costs more.

**The court.** King Aldren rules from the palace on the rise above the river. He is warm and hospitable, remembers how everyone takes their tea, and is famously unwilling to sign anything that might upset anyone. Marshal Garran Holt keeps the roads, the garrisons and the Assembly timetable, to the minute. Magister Corvin keeps the royal seal and the exact wording of the law.

**The city**
- The palace on the rise, with its offices and kitchens in the back courts.
- The market square: stalls, the market cross, the procession route, and the Corn Exchange, where grain factors trade, chalk up prices and keep the wagon lists.
- The granary quarter: the King's Granary, warehouses, porters' lodgings and a watch house.
- The river stairs, down to the docks and the wharves, with the Wharf Road winding down at the downriver end for wagons.
- The Shambles, the butchers' quarter across the city from the river, where porters' families rent rooms over the shops.
- The north gate, where the city keeps what it would rather not look at: the Mending House inside it, the suicides' pit outside it.

**Why it's like this**: Caerwyn is roads, courts and garrisons. The palace buys first and the court runs the roads; the river carries away whatever pays better downriver. Most of the city works for one or the other: at a desk in the palace, or with a hook on the river.

**Who does well out of it**: the palace and its officers, the grain factors and the Saltmere buyers on the wharves, and, this week, every innkeeper with a bed.
**Who pays for it**: porters, carters and granary rats. A porter earns about eight pennies a day, and the price of bread is the first thing anyone on the river stairs will tell you.

**The rules, and who keeps them**
- The City Watch keeps the King's peace in the streets. Officers of the royal household answer to the palace: the watch may not lay hands on one without a warrant under the royal seal, unless he's caught in the act.
- The river stairs are the river watch's patch.
- The palace bells ring the hours, the half hours and the quarters for the whole city.
- The Mending House takes in strays and wayward children and mends them with porridge, hymns and picking oakum. Every granary rat would sooner take their chances with the goblins.

**Everyday things**
- Money: twelve silver pennies to the shilling, five shillings to the crown, so a silver crown is more than a week's wages. Caerwyn's pennies carry the King's face, and the chandlers want to see it.
- Magic is Nine Furrows business: weather, wards and grain. Nobody in Caerwyn talks to the dead, and the dead stay dead, which people find a comfort.

**What people say, and who says it**
- Anyone with a desk at the palace: "After the Assembly."
- The river stairs: visitors notice the gilt; the city notices the bread.
- Everyone, about anything that goes missing: "lost to goblins".

**What's happening now**: the eve of the Assembly. There's bunting on every rope that will hold it, the watch is out lining the procession route, delegations' servants are everywhere, and prices are up, bread most of all. How things stand at this hour, and what the town is saying, is in [Caerwyn now](Caerwyn%20now.md).

campaign.lore/World/Centennial Assembly.md:
---
summary: "The Centennial Assembly at Caerwyn: why the kingdoms meet every hundred years and what Edric's Concord has to do with it, the four delegations and their banners (Caerwyn's open hand, the Nine Furrows wheat-sheaf, Kläggenheim's axes, Saltmere's salt-gull), who wants what from it and who resents it, the Treasury's levy and the Marshal's arms order, the order of procession with the Purveyor's grain cart, and the week bell by bell: the eve, the delegations' dinner, procession morning at the ninth bell, the feast, and 'After the Assembly'."
type: "world"
visibility: "public"
---
# The Centennial Assembly

Every hundred years the kingdoms come to one court and say, in public, who their common sovereign is. This winter they've come to King Aldren's palace in Caerwyn, and nothing else in the city gets done.

**Why they must**: the custom is older than anyone's grandmother's grandmother. This is the first Assembly since King Edric the Peacemaker made his Concord a generation ago. Under the Concord each kingdom keeps its own rulers and laws, pays tribute, and brings its quarrels to the King instead of to war. Recognising Aldren renews it.

**The delegations, all arrived, and their banners**
- **Caerwyn**, the host (roads, courts and garrisons): King Edric's open hand.
- **Nine Furrows** (wizards of the ancient university, who see to weather, wards and grain): the wheat-sheaf.
- **Kläggenheim** (dwarven miners and engineers, and old King Gurt): crossed axes.
- **Saltmere** (ships, warehouses, insurance and credit, and Prince Peregrine): the salt-gull. The heron on the sign of the Heron warehouse is one Saltmere grain factor's own house mark, not Saltmere's.

**Who wants what from it**
- **King Aldren**: to be recognised again as common sovereign under the Concord, with nobody upset.
- **The delegations**: their laws kept and their tribute argued down, and to be seen to argue it.
- **Marshal Holt**: everything on time, to the minute.
- **The Purveyor's office**: the feast is theirs to supply, grain crisis or no grain crisis, and they mean to be thanked for it.
- **The city**: cheaper bread and a day off. It is getting a procession.

**Who does well out of it**: innkeepers and lodging-house keepers, chandlers and bunting-sellers, anyone with brandy to sell to a delegation's steward, and anyone who'll scrub or turn a spit in the palace kitchens, where extra hands are fed.
**Who pays, and resents it**: travellers paying the Treasury's shilling a head; carters and drovers paying the Marshal's two pennies a weapon on a road where goblins shoot oxen; porters and lightermen, whose docks shut for a day without pay; the watch, lining the route through the night; and anyone who has noticed the gilt and the bread on the same day.

**The rules, and who keeps them**
- **The Treasury's Assembly levy**: a shilling a head, "to defray the costs of the Centennial", collected from "such travellers as are able and willing" at the gates and at Garrow's toll bridge.
- **Marshal Holt's arms order**: two pennies for each weapon borne on the King's Road in Assembly week. Weapons peace-bonded with red cord and wax go free.
- **The timetable** is the Marshal's. The procession leaves at the ninth bell whatever anyone has said.
- **"After the Assembly"**: every office in the palace gives the same answer to every request this week.

**The week, bell by bell**
- **The eve**: every official is at the palace, the whole watch is out lining the procession route, and rehearsals run in the Great Hall. The docks shut tomorrow for the procession, so the river pays off early tonight.
- **The eve, after dark**: the palace is shut to everyone but the delegations' dinner and the procession rehearsal. The watch lines the route all night.
- **Procession morning**: the delegations form up under their banners in the palace courtyard. At the ninth bell the procession leaves the palace gate and winds through the market square: the three visiting delegations under their banners, then the Purveyor's party fourth with a grain cart in garlands, "for the people's confidence", and then the court, and the King under Caerwyn's open hand.
- **Then** the Assembly sits in the Great Hall, and after it comes the feast.
- **After the Assembly**: officials, the watch surgeon and the granary warden can be found again, the Assizes sit, and a case can be laid before the King, who signs nothing that might upset anyone.

**What people say, and who says it**
- The delegations' servants: everyone has come to recognise one sovereign and argue about the wording.
- Watchmen on the route: which end of the route is the beginning.
- Porters on the river stairs: a day's pay lost for a procession they'll be standing in the cold to watch.
- The palace kitchens: the cushions for the Assembly seats, which haven't arrived, and the under-purveyor for linen, who is having a very bad week about them.

**What's happening now**: the delegations have arrived and the route is being lined. The procession leaves at the ninth bell tomorrow. How things stand at this hour is in [Caerwyn now](Caerwyn%20now.md).

campaign.lore/World/City Watch (truth).md:
---
summary: "GM only: why Captain Bunce closed Prout's death as a suicide at Master Sallow's request, what he owes the Purveyor's office (Assembly rations, quarter-day hampers, a promised place at the head of the procession), what he does if the clerk is signed in as a murder and when the case is pressed, what would prove his part, and whether anyone in the watch is bent."
type: "world"
visibility: "gm"
---
# The City Watch: the truth

Captain Bunce closed Wendell Prout's death as self-murder because Master Sallow asked him to, and he didn't ask why. He knows nothing of the murder or the racket. He finds Sallow a gentleman who gets things done:
- Sallow arranged for the Purveyor's office to feed the watch on Assembly duty: bread, cheese and small beer for every man on the route.
- A hamper of palace pies reaches the Captain's table every quarter-day, by Sallow's kindness.
- Sallow has promised to see that the Captain rides at the head of the procession.

**What he does**
- If a sergeant signs the clerk in as a murder, his first instinct is to make it go away without fuss. Kell's report is wanted "after the Assembly", and he mentions it to Sallow at the palace, as one gentleman to another, because the office asked to have it closed.
- Pressed on the case, he tries the same instinct again. Once it can't be made to go away, his second instinct is to have suspected Sallow all along, and he says so to anyone who'll listen.
- He won't cross the palace without the King's say-so.

**What would prove his part**: his own written order, which Corporal Tull carries and will show to anyone who doubts him: "The death of W. Prout, clerk, to be closed as self-murder, without fuss, at the request of Master J. Sallow of the Royal Purveyor's office." It names who asked. It doesn't make the Captain anything worse than obliging.

**Who knows**: the Captain knows only that Sallow wanted it closed quietly. Tull thinks it a rum business when the Purveyor's office cares how a clerk gets filed, and keeps that to himself. Kell thinks the Captain says yes to gentlemen.

Nobody else in the watch is in Sallow's pay. They're honest, tired and underpaid.

**In motion**: what the Captain does next, step by step, is in [What's in motion](Fronts.md) under "The Captain's book".

# The City Watch

The watch keeps the King's peace in Caerwyn's streets: a Captain who likes a parade, a handful of sergeants, corporals and constables, and never enough of any of them. Rain capes and truncheons, and notebooks for the sergeants.

**Why it's like this**
- The city pays for the watch and has never paid for much of one.
- The palace looks after its own. Officers of the royal household answer to the palace, so the watch keeps the streets and leaves the palace's people to the palace.
- The Captain, Aubrey Bunce, is a fine figure on a horse, fond of a parade, the palace and a quiet life. His favourite words are "without fuss": he likes a short report, and a case closed before it's opened.

**Who does well out of it**: the Captain, who gets a quiet life and a hamper from the Purveyor's office every quarter-day (the men have never seen more of it than the straw); and the palace's officers, whom the watch can't touch.
**Who pays for it**: a sergeant who signs a death in against the Captain's word, and answers to him for it; the dead nobody signs for; constables lining the route all night on watch pay; and the river stairs, which the watch leaves to the river watch.

**The rules, and who keeps them**
- **The Captain's book**: every death in the city goes in it as natural, accident, self-murder or murder, and the Captain's word stands. A sergeant may sign a body in as a murder instead, and answers to the Captain for it.
- **A murder** goes to the cold room at the watch house to wait for the watch surgeon. **A suicide** goes into the pit outside the north gate, under quicklime, by sundown on the day it's found. No grave, no stone, and after that nobody asks again.
- **Arrests**: a sergeant who sees a crime done may arrest whoever does it, gentleman or not, out loud and with the proper words. Anyone else can be taken up on evidence: his own admission, a witness who'll swear, a wound that matches. An officer of the royal household, the Purveyor's office included, can't be touched without a warrant under the royal seal unless he's caught in the act.
- **Children** the watch takes up go to the Mending House by the north gate.
- **The river stairs** belong to the river watch, which walks them in fours after dark, or not at all.

**How it touches ordinary people**: the dead-cart (a handcart with a long ladder lashed on top, pushed by two constables, with a bell); watchmen walking in pairs after dark; and a bell on the watch-house counter to ring when nobody's behind it.

**What people say, and who says it**
- Nan Quill, and the river stairs with her: in thirty years the watch has never once come down the stairs for a gentleman.
- The stairs: Sergeant Kell writes everything down, takes nothing from anybody, and is still a sergeant because her reports say what happened.
- Lightermen: the watch are bluebottles who fine you a shilling for mooring where everyone moors.
- Granary rats: the watch works for good coats, and believes a good coat over a granary kid every time.
- Corporal Tull: an order stands until the Captain writes a new one, or the Sarge signs for something and takes it on herself.

**What's happening now**: the whole watch is out lining the Assembly route, hanging bunting, moving carts and chasing pigs, and it stays out through the night. The Captain is at the palace seeing to the route, and the watch surgeon is on duty at the palace. Until after the Assembly nobody can be spared for anything else.

# What's in motion

Caerwyn gets on with its own troubles whether or not the investigator is looking. Each front is someone, or something, that wants something, with a clock of steps.

**How to use it**
- A step ticks at a scene boundary when play has made it true or its time has come, never because it would be dramatic. Tick it (`- [x]`). Strike out a step that play has made meaningless, and say why.
- Nobody acts on what they couldn't know: each step says who learns what, and from whom.
- A step shows once, as something seen or someone who'd say it, sign before consequence: mostly in the interludes and the first replies of the next scene. One visible step per front per boundary, and no more than two fronts surfacing in a scene.
- A front changes circumstances inside the scenes the player is in. It never adds a scene, a route or an ending, and never answers a stakes question. What anyone could see or hear goes in [Caerwyn now](Caerwyn%20now.md); the why stays here.

## The Purveyor's man
**Who**: Master Josiah Sallow, under-purveyor for grain, with Big Hobb Mallory, the Crake brothers (hired for the Heron's wharf on loading nights), a lantern-boy, and the Heron's people, who are his by pay, not loyalty.
**Wants**: the clerk Prout's business closed for good, tidily; tonight's barge away on the ebb and tonight's page initialled; to walk in the procession and be thanked for feeding the feast; in time, the Royal Purveyor's chain.
**Resources**: the office's signature and keys; the Captain's goodwill (hampers, Assembly rations, a promised place at the head of the procession); an order of sale for "condemned stock, lawfully sold"; heron silver; the Crakes; the river.
**Limits**: he never fights while someone can be paid to, and never goes down the river stairs. He's careful with paper and careless with coins, smells, servants and children. He doesn't know about the page in the boot, Cob in the loft, Moll's crown being traceable office silver, or Scrope being Prout's friend.

- [x] Prout is filed as self-murder at Sallow's request, before anyone has looked. *Shows as*: Corporal Tull's written order.
- [ ] **If Prout goes into the Captain's book as a murder** (the granary ends "The case is made" or "Murder by persons unknown"; `prout_death` "murder, Sallow named" or "murder, unnamed"): by evening the Captain has mentioned it to Sallow at the palace, as one gentleman to another. Sergeant Kell, the one he lent the King's investigator, has signed the clerk in as a murder, and he'll have it straightened out after the Assembly. Sallow is wary, not warned: he knows who is asking, not what they have. Before the tenth bell he sends the Crakes down the river stairs to find out who's been asking after his porter, and has a second lantern hung at the Heron's land door. *Shows as*: two big men alike as bollards at the pump on the stairs, asking who's been asking about Big Hobb (they're barred from the Rat); later, two lanterns at the Heron's land door.
- [ ] **If the wheat-ear crown is shown or spent where the office will hear of it** (the palace, its kitchens, the Corn Exchange, or a shopkeeper who sends word up the hill): Sallow learns that a granary girl kept his coin. *Shows as*: his yawning lantern-boy in the granary quarter, asking the granary rats where the girl in the shawl sleeps. If nobody stops it, a Crake comes asking after dark.
- [ ] **The loading night.** If Hobb ran to him from the Rat (`sallow_warned`), Sallow knows the King's investigator and a watch sergeant are asking about the loft: he comes at the midnight bell sharp and hurrying, with Hobb at his heels and the Crakes walking the wharf ahead of him, and wants the true book sewn into oilcloth and aboard the Patience first of all; Hobb, who panicked once, is a loose end now, and when the last sack is down the Crakes walk him home along the wharf, by the water. If Hobb simply isn't at the river door (taken in at the Rat), Sallow finds his porter missing at the bell, and that alone makes him wary: the Crakes look along the wharf, and the loading is hurried. Otherwise he comes on time, finds fault, initials the page and takes his share. At the second bell after midnight the Patience casts off on the ebb with the King's grain, unless someone stops her. *Shows as*: the Crakes on the wharf before the bell; the Master early, or asking after his porter; by morning the Heron shut and swept, and the empty wheat-ear sacks in the river, weighted with stones.
- [ ] **Procession morning**, unless he's in a cell or has fled: he walks fourth with the Purveyor's party and the garlanded grain cart. If he knows the true book has left the Heron, he's at the palace before dawn to get his story in first: the order of sale, "condemned stock", a ledger stolen by intruders, and a word with the Captain. *Shows as*: Sallow in the long gallery with the Purveyor's party and a folio of papers, courteous and ready.

**Doom**: the office "saves" the Assembly feast with the King's own grain, bought back at Assembly prices on credit his friends downriver arrange. He's thanked for it, and has the chain when old Sir Gilbert goes. Prout stays in the pit, or in the book as persons unknown.
**Stakes**: Will Hobb live to swear to what he did? Will Moll keep her crown, and her neck? Will Kell's notebook count for more than the Captain's book?
**Ticked by**: `hanged-clerk` case-made and open-case (the other endings leave him unhurried tonight: one lantern, on time, bored); `drowned-rat` hobb-fled and taken-in; `heron-warehouse` barge-sails, proof-taken and caught.
**If he's arrested at the Heron** (`caught-in-the-act`), strike the front out. In its place, the office closes ranks the next morning: his order of sale and Sir Gilbert's name on it, while the Captain tells anyone who'll listen that he suspected the man all along. *Shows as*: the Purveyor's party walking without him, the grain cart still in garlands. **If the Heron burns or the barge sinks** (`up-in-smoke`), his grain is gone, and he blames the goblins, then the fire, then the factor.

## The Captain's book
**Who**: Captain Aubrey Bunce, commander of the watch, with Corporal Tull, the constables and the dead-cart.
**Wants**: the route lined and everything else closed before the bells, without fuss; to ride at the head of the procession, as Master Sallow promised him; a short report and a quiet life.
**Resources**: the Captain's book, where his word stands; the whole watch, all of it on the route; the cells and the cold room; the Assizes after the Assembly.
**Limits**: his men are honest, tired and underpaid, and none of them is bent. He won't cross the palace without the King's say-so. He isn't bought, just obliging (see [the City Watch: the truth](City%20Watch%20%28truth%29.md)).

- [x] Prout is called a suicide before anyone has looked, and the dead-cart is ordered for noon.
- [ ] **Noon on the eve**: the dead-cart comes. Unless a sergeant signs Prout in as a murder, he goes out of the north gate and into the pit under quicklime by sundown, and nobody asks again. *Shows as*: the dead-cart's bell going through the market towards the north gate.
- [ ] **If a sergeant signs Prout in as a murder**, with no granary child taken in for it, he goes to the cold room under a sheet to wait for the surgeon. Tull tells the Captain on the route by the afternoon bells. The Captain's first instinct is to make it go away without fuss: he wants Kell's report "after the Assembly", and he mentions it to Master Sallow, which ticks *The Purveyor's man*. *Shows as*: a constable sent with the Captain's word for Kell; granary porters telling anyone that a sergeant signed the clerk in over the Captain's word.
- [ ] **If a granary child is taken in for it instead**, the Captain gladly files a murder that embarrasses nobody, and nobody troubles Master Sallow with it (*The Purveyor's man* doesn't tick). *Shows as*: the market saying a granary brat did it, and the granary rats saying otherwise, loudly.
- [ ] **Through the night** the whole watch lines the route, the river watch with it. Whatever happens at the wharves happens without the watch: Kell's whistle brings Kell. Anyone put in the cells tonight is locked in and left, with the key in the pocket of whoever brought him. *Shows as*: nobody behind the watch-house counter.
- [ ] **Procession morning**: the Captain rides in the procession, put out that it isn't at its head (the Marshal refused the Purveyor's office's request for that). If an officer of the household was taken up in the night, his second instinct takes over: he has suspected the man all along, and says so to anyone. *Shows as*: the Captain on his horse in the palace courtyard.

**Doom**: the Captain's book stands. Prout lies in the pit as a suicide, Kell's report is read after the Assembly and filed, and the Captain rides in the procession, grateful to the Purveyor's office for the rations.
**Stakes**: Will Kell's notebook count for more than the Captain's book? Will anyone in the watch go down the river stairs for a gentleman?
**Ticked by**: every `hanged-clerk` ending; `drowned-rat` taken-in; `heron-warehouse` caught-in-the-act.

## Dear bread
**What**: the price of bread and the city's patience: nobody's plan, and everybody's grievance. Behind it are the poor harvest, the palace buying first, the "lost" wagons, the factors who chalk up the price, the bakers who shrink the loaf before they raise it, and Saltmere barges going downriver full. Porters on eight pennies a day pay for it, and so do carters and granary rats. The factors, the Saltmere buyers and the office do well out of it.
**Clock**: a tug-of-war. Time and bad news fill it; good news empties it.

- [x] Tuppence a loaf, a penny dearer than at harvest. "Lost to goblins" stopped being funny about a fortnight ago.
- [ ] **The noon and evening bells on the eve**: the Corn Exchange chalks up a rise each time, and by evening the tuppenny loaf is smaller. *Shows as*: the price board, with something rude written beside it by evening; Nan's eel stew thinner; Cob hungrier.
- [ ] **The afternoon of the eve**: a preacher at the market cross calls dear bread a judgement on the bunting. *Shows as*: the sermon, preached to a bread queue.
- [ ] **After dark on the eve**: a crowd at the Corn Exchange board, and a cabbage thrown at a Purveyor's wagon taking flour up to the palace. *Shows as*: by morning, a dented wheat-ear canvas at the palace service entrance.
- [ ] **Procession morning**: threepence at the bakers who open, and people along the route who've come to shout "lost to goblins!" at the Purveyor's grain cart. *Shows as*: the shouting, heard through the King's windows.

**Doom**: a bread riot on the procession route, in front of the delegations.
**Ticks down if** people hear the King's "lost" grain has been found (an under-purveyor taken up at the wharves, or the King acting on the proof): then the crowd asks the grain cart "Found the goblins, then?" **Ticks up if** grain burns or sinks (`up-in-smoke`): "lost to goblins" becomes "lost to fire", and bread jumps.
**Stakes**: Who will Caerwyn blame: the goblins, Saltmere or the office? Will the procession pass without a riot?
**Ticked by**: time, at each boundary on the eve; `heron-warehouse` up-in-smoke (up) and caught-in-the-act (down, by morning); `kings-morning` justice (down).

## The Assembly week
**Who**: Marshal Garran Holt, who keeps the timetable to the minute and commands the palace guard; King Aldren, the host; the Treasury and its levy; the Purveyor's office and its feast.
**Wants**: the procession out of the gate at the ninth bell, and the Concord renewed without a scene in front of the delegations. The King, above all, wants not to have to decide anything that might upset anyone.
**Underneath**: the Treasury is waiting on Saltmere's credit, which was coming upriver with a courier and hasn't come: Sallow paid the goblins to take her at the ford (see [the Grain Crisis: the truth](Grain%20Crisis%20%28truth%29.md)), unless she got through (`warren-hostage` completed the `saltmere-courier` quest). That's why the levy is collected so keenly, and why the office's promise to see the feast fed is so welcome at the palace.

- [x] **The eve, morning**: the delegations have arrived, every official is at the palace, and the whole watch is lining the route. "After the Assembly."
- [ ] **The eve, afternoon**: rehearsals in the Great Hall. The gate takes written messages for the Marshal, and he reads them by evening. He acts at first light on whatever he can act on without the King's word: he sends a page for whoever wrote, and puts a guard on whatever they named. He keeps his guard at the palace while the delegations dine, and arrests no officer of the household on a letter. *Shows as*: gate guards who've been told the King will see the investigator in the morning.
- [ ] **The eve, after dark**: the palace is shut to everyone but the delegations' dinner and the procession rehearsal. *Shows as*: lit windows, carriages, a band rehearsing.
- [ ] **Procession morning**: half an hour before the ninth bell the King, half into his robes, sees the investigator in his dressing room. At the ninth bell the procession leaves the gate, whatever has been said; then the Assembly sits, and then the feast. *Shows as*: a palace page at first light; the bells.

**Doom**: everything goes off on time. The Concord is renewed over a feast the office fed with the King's own grain, and anything that might upset anyone waits until after the Assembly.
**Stakes**: Will the King decide anything before the ninth bell?
**Ticked by**: time only. The public timetable is in [The Centennial Assembly](Centennial%20Assembly.md).

## The river tonight
**What**: the river in winter spate, and the docks on the night before they shut for the procession. The Saltmere factors want their barges loaded and away before then. The porters and lightermen are paid off early with no work tomorrow. The river watch, whose patch the stairs are, is up on the route.

- [x] The river is high, fast and cold, and Saltmere barges have been loading at the Heron by night all month.
- [ ] **Dusk on the eve**: the river pays off early, and since tomorrow's wages are lost, tonight's are drunk. *Shows as*: paid-off porters crowding the stairs; the Rat packed.
- [ ] **The eleventh bell**: the night shift goes down, and the Heron's gang and its hoist man are due at the river door. *Shows as*: lanterns going down the stairs; the Heron's hoist working.
- [ ] **Midnight to the second bell after**: the tide turns, and fog comes off the water. At the second bell the ebb runs and the Patience casts off. *Shows as*: bargees singling up their lines; a stern lantern going downriver.
- [ ] **Procession morning**: the docks are shut and the wharves quiet. What went into the river in the night turns up downriver, or doesn't. *Shows as*: empty wharves; mudlarks at the low-water mark.

**Doom**: whatever and whoever goes into the river tonight is gone by morning. Every Assembly somebody falls in.
**Stakes**: Will the Patience sail? Will anyone go into the river who shouldn't?
**Ticked by**: time; `heron-warehouse` barge-sails and up-in-smoke.

## Bills still to come due
A hard ending or a daft act sends its bill later. Each has an "if" and where it will show; play adds more, and strikes them out when they're paid.
- **If Nan threw the investigator out of the Rat** (`thrown-out`): by the eleventh bell the stairs have it that the sergeant's friend got Manners. If they go back, they're barred until they've paid for whatever broke, at Nan's valuation.
- **If a granary child was taken in on the investigator's word** (`wrong-man`): the other one has gone to ground, and every granary rat knows whose word it was.
- **If the investigator was thrown in the river or locked up at the Heron** (`caught`): Sallow believes he's rid of them. If they walk into the palace in the morning, the first look on his face is the true one.
- **If the Heron burned or the Patience sank** (`up-in-smoke`): somebody must explain it on the morning of the Assembly, and the Marshal asks before the King does.

# The Grain Crisis: the truth

There are goblins on the King's Road, but they aren't what's taking the wagons.

## The racket
- **Who**: Master Josiah Sallow, under-purveyor for grain in the Royal Purveyor's office. A good coat, a silver-topped cane, a wheat-ear signet ring and too much lavender water. His muscle is Big Hobb Mallory, a dock-porter the size of a door; on the wharf he hires the Crake brothers.
- **How**: palace grain wagons on the King's Road are written off in the Royal Granary Roll as "lost to goblins", each countersigned "J. Sallow, for the Royal Purveyor". The grain goes by night, still in the palace's wheat-ear sacks, down the Wharf Road to the Heron warehouse, where it's re-sacked under the heron mark of a Saltmere grain factor and sold downriver. If anyone asks, it's condemned stock lawfully sold, on an order of sale in Sallow's own hand. Nobody has ever asked.
- **The true book**: Sallow and the factor don't trust each other, so both insisted on a ledger kept by a clerk they both pay, Mister Lemuel Scrope. It records every "lost" wagon by its Roll number, with Sallow's initials on every page.
- **The goblins**: Sallow pays the hedge-goblins of the burnt mill to be seen on the road and to raid now and then, so the story holds. He pays them in heron pennies from the factor's cashbox, and since the book has to balance, Scrope enters it: on the last page of each month, in the same careful hand, "Hedge-folk, the usual: forty heron pennies." The book answers Prout's question. To the goblins Sallow is a longlegs in a grey hood who smells of lavender.
- **Why**: money, and standing. An Assembly short of grain and money is one the Purveyor's office gets to save, and Sallow means to be the man who saves it, with grain he happens to have, and to be thanked with the Royal Purveyor's chain.
- **The Saltmere courier** (background): in the same grey hood, Sallow paid Chief Gubbin to snatch Hester Quayle, the Saltmere courier, at a ford on the King's Road. Her sealed letter is Saltmere's credit for the King's treasury: the loan that pays for the Assembly. Unless she got through, the Treasury is short, which is why the levy is collected so keenly.

## Prout
Wendell Prout, under-clerk of the Granary Roll, read the Corn Exchange's wagon lists, where every load sold in the city is weighed and entered, and found the "lost" wagons weighed in at the Heron two days after each loss, as condemned palace stock sold by order of the Purveyor's office. He pencilled the weights beside the entries, razored the page out of the Roll and sewed it into his boot. He asked Sergeant Kell how a clerk reports false entries, and wrote to the Royal Purveyor through the proper channels. Sallow opens the Royal Purveyor's letters. In the small hours of the eve of the Assembly, Sallow and Hobb caught him in the tally loft, killed him and hoisted him on the sack hoist to look like a suicide. At first light Sallow paid a granary girl to say she'd seen him jump, then asked the Watch Captain to close it quietly.

## Who knows what
- **Sallow**: all of it. **Hobb**: the murder, the wagons and the Heron's night routine. He carries a brass token for its river door.
- **The Heron's people** (Hep Grist and her gang, Saul Tench, Scrope) know whose grain they're handling and have never said so. Scrope knows why Wendell Prout is dead.
- **Gubbin**: a grey hood, lavender and heron pennies, but no name.
- **Abel Fennick**, the Corn Exchange's clerk, let Prout read the wagon lists. He doesn't know why Prout wanted them.
- **Nan Quill** knows the gentleman's name and what the porters say about the Heron's grain, and won't sell it.
- **Cob** heard the murder from his nest in the loft. **Moll** took Sallow's silver and heard his name. **Kell** knows Prout came to her. **The Captain** knows only that Sallow wanted it closed quietly.

## The proof
- Prout's page, and the Roll chained to the tally desk with the page razored out.
- Moll's wheat-ear crown: office purse silver.
- Heron pennies, new this month and paid out only at the Heron: in Nan's jar marked FOREIGN, in Dilly's winnings, in Cob's pocket, and in the goblins' warren.
- Hobb's token and his word, and the words of the Heron's people if they'll swear for the Crown.
- The Corn Exchange's wagon lists: the "lost" wagons weighed in at the Heron.
- Sallow's own order of sale, which calls "condemned stock, lawfully sold" the very wagons his countersignature in the Roll calls "lost to goblins".
- The true book, which would hang him.

## In motion
Sallow's next moves, and what each looks like when it happens, are in [What's in motion](Fronts.md) under "The Purveyor's man". On the eve he's at the palace until near midnight, then at the Heron at the midnight bell to see the Patience loaded and initial the night's page.

# The Grain Crisis

Bread in Caerwyn is tuppence a loaf, a penny dearer than at harvest, and a porter earns about eight pennies a day. Ask anyone why and they'll say goblins.

**Why it's dear**
- The harvest was poor after a wet summer, and the Nine Furrows granaries are thin.
- The palace buys first. By the King's right of purveyance the Royal Purveyor's office buys at the King's price, so farmers bring the palace what they must and sell the rest where it fetches more.
- The palace's own grain keeps going missing. A dozen wagons bound for the King's Granary have been "lost to goblins" on the King's Road this past month, each one written off in the Royal Granary Roll and countersigned by the Purveyor's office. What the palace loses on the road, it buys again in the market.
- Saltmere pays better than Caerwyn, and Saltmere barges have been going downriver full.
- The Assembly feast must be fed regardless. The office says it has the matter in hand.

**Who does well out of it**: the grain factors at the Corn Exchange, who chalk up a new price twice a day; the Saltmere buyers on the wharves, whose barges go downriver low in the water; and the Purveyor's office, which expects to be thanked for feeding the feast at all.
**Who pays for it**: porters, carters and granary rats, for whom a loaf is a quarter of a day's work; farmers, who sell to the King at the King's price; the granary porters, with bays standing empty and less to carry; and the Treasury, which writes off every lost wagon and this week is collecting a shilling a head from travellers.

**The rules, and who keeps them**
- Palace grain lost on the road is written off in the Royal Granary Roll, and the Purveyor's office countersigns the entry. Nobody else checks.
- The Corn Exchange chalks the day's prices on its board at the noon bell and again at the evening bell. The factors set them, and the Exchange's clerk chalks them up.
- A baker keeps the loaf at tuppence as long as he can by making it smaller. The market warden fines short weight, and this week he's at the palace with every other official.
- The watch keeps the King's peace, not the price of bread.

**How it touches ordinary people**: queues at the bakers from first light; a smaller loaf for the same tuppence; thinner stew on the river stairs. And "lost to goblins" is now what Caerwyn says about anything that goes missing, whether it's a hat, a husband or the rent. It stopped being funny about a fortnight ago.

**What people say, and who says it**
- Carters: they won't take the King's Road after dark without a patrol, and there are no patrols.
- Farmers at market: they've never seen goblins carry off a whole wagon of wheat, and wonder where a goblin would sell one.
- Dock-porters: Saltmere barges are taking grain downriver while Caerwyn goes short. They take Saltmere's money for loading them all the same.
- The palace kitchens: the feast will be fed because the office says so, and the office's word is stamped on its pennies.
- The preacher at the market cross: dear bread is a judgement on the bunting.

**What's happening now**: the Corn Exchange has chalked the price up every day this week. The hour-by-hour state of things is in [Caerwyn now](Caerwyn%20now.md).

## Read when relevant
- [Caerwyn now](Caerwyn%20now.md) — read for today's price of bread and the talk around town at this hour

- [The Royal Purveyor's office](Royal%20Purveyor's%20Office.md) — read for who buys the palace's grain and signs the write-offs
- [The Centennial Assembly](Centennial%20Assembly.md) — read for the feast and the city's Assembly preparations
